name: garak
what: An open-source LLM vulnerability scanner ("nmap for LLMs") that runs probe families against a model or LLM-backed application — prompt injection, encoding-based injection, jailbreaks (DAN-style), data leakage/training-data replay, package hallucination, XSS-style exfiltration, toxicity — and scores each with detectors.
when: Before you approve or scale an internal LLM app, RAG chatbot or agent endpoint (your own Azure OpenAI/Foundry, Bedrock, Hugging Face or REST-exposed deployment), and as a regression gate after prompt, model or guardrail changes. It complements governance: the approved-inventory says what may run, garak shows how the app fails. Only test endpoints you own or are contracted to test; probing third-party SaaS chat products is outside most terms of service.
cost_note: The tool is free; every probe generates real model calls, so API-hosted targets incur token costs (default 10 generations per prompt).
example: Install in an isolated environment (Python 3.11+): `python -m pip install -U garak`, then `garak --list_probes` to see probe families.

Scope narrowly first — for an OpenAI-API-compatible test deployment: `export OPENAI_API_KEY=<test-key>` then `python3 -m garak --target_type openai --target_name <model> --spec probes.encoding` (encoding-based prompt injection).

For your own LLM app behind an HTTP API, use the REST generator (`--target_type rest`) with a short config describing the endpoint, request template and response field (see the rest generator reference).

Add `probes.promptinject`, `probes.dan`, `probes.leakreplay` and `probes.packagehallucination` once the baseline run is stable; run against the full application (system prompt + guardrails), not just the bare model.
Read results per probe/detector (FAIL rate per generations); keep the per-run JSONL report and hit log as evidence and diff them between releases.
pitfalls: A clean garak run is not proof of safety — probes are a sample of known techniques, and detectors produce false positives and negatives; triage hits manually.
Running every probe by default against a paid API can be slow and expensive; use --spec to scope.
Never point it at production endpoints with real user data in context or at vendors' consumer chat services; use a dedicated test deployment and a test key.
Indirect prompt injection via documents and tool/MCP responses needs scenario testing beyond a model-level scan.
